p: Ryan, I have a question for you. So, I don’t know if you saw the testimony earlier, but I asked a question about the transparency portal on the website.
Yes.
So, if– at another point in time, if you could call my office and get back to me about what you see there, I want to follow up on that.
Absolutely, we’d love to follow up on the price comparison tool.

Okay, great. Thank you very much. This panel is excused. Thank you. Alright, next panel is Robert Acevedo, Elizabeth Valdez, Mike Schweinsberg [sp?], Dr. Robert– oh, I’m sorry– Robert– Robin, I’m sorry. I can’t read the writing. Recant, Dr. Robin Recant. Yes? No? Michael Kush or Michal Kush [sp?]? Jordan Rosenthal [sp?]? Sure. Juan Pinzum [sp?]. Is Juan here?

Yes, he is, okay. Okay, Robert Acevedo, why don’t you go first?

My name is Robert Acevedo and I’m a member of Disabled in Action of Metropolitan New York. A little description. I use a wheelchair and I’m wearing a red shirt with brown pants. The Mayor’s Office for People with Disabilities has long been chronically underfunded, limiting its ability to serve as an effective liaison between New Yorkers with disabilities and city agencies. As a result, city services, programs, activities and newly-built facilities like the Hunter’s Point Library in Queens had to often been planned and delivered without sufficient accessibility, producing federally non-compliant outcomes and exposing the city to costly litigation. Oh. An increase in the funding today would enable the office to intervene at the earliest stages of program and facility planning, ensuring accessibility is built in from the outset and preventing litigation, higher long-term costs. Other major cities invest significantly more in their disability offices. It is time for New York City to make a

comparable commitment. We respectfully request a significant and sustained increase in the funding for the Mayor’s Office for People with Disabilities so the city can fulfill its legal obligations and ensure full inclusion for all residents. Thank you.
Thank you very much. Elizabeth?

Good afternoon. My name is Elizabeth Valdez and I’m the Systems Advocate at the Brooklyn Center for Independence of the Disabled. I’m here today to urge the Council to make a significantly stronger commitment in the city budget to the Mayor’s Office for People with Disabilities. For far too long this office has been underfunded since its inception in 1968 and through its various forms over the years. It has never been given the level of investment needed to truly meet the needs of New Yorkers with disabilities. Today, we have an opportunity to change that. With new Council leadership, the creation of a Disabilities Committee, a new administration, and a new Commissioner at MOPD, this is the moment to reverse decades of neglect. People with disabilities

interact with city government every single day, whether it’s living independently, accessing transportation, securing and maintaining accessible housing, or simply participating fully in our communities. We rely on city systems to function effectively and equitably. But when those systems fail us when there are communication breakdowns, accessibility barriers or a lack of understanding about disability services, the consequences are severe. Too often individuals are pushed into nursing homes, shelters, or sub-standard congregate housing. These outcomes are not only devastating for individuals and families, they’re also far more costly for the city and state. Despite the growing needs of our community, MODP’s budget has not kept pace with the city’s overall budget. In fact, in the proposed 2026/2027 budget MOPD would see no increase from the $678,657 it received last year unless council takes action. Increased funding for MOPD is not just necessary, it is also an investment in equity, efficiency and dignity.
Thank you very much. Mike Schweinsburg.

Kindly. My name’s Mike Schweinsburg. I’m the President of the 504 Democratic Club. I am an old man with graying brown hair and glasses and a checked rust-colored suit and a blue shirt. Okay. We are the largest minority by far. Yet, today, I’ve heard 10 percent of the population, a million of us, don’t go by the decennial census which deliberately undercounts us. Check out the CDC website that did an extensive survey every year. And the last year they were allowed to publish their findings was 24, and they pegged us at 28.7 percent of the population. Excuse me, 28.7 percent of adults. So they’re not counting our kids. None of our kids were over 30 percent of the population. We are totally intersectional and found in every single segment of society. We are the most marginalized of every marginalized group and 60 percent of our population come from communities of color. We maintain when you lift up the disability community you are raising all marginalized communities from the bottom up. You need to understand that, because here comes our budget ask. With regards to the budget for MOPD, When we came up

with a figure of $100 million for the first year for MOPD. it of course, seemed quite reasonable to us, $5 a head. Those who have seen MOPD’s offices know there are a great many unused cubicles in spaces that could be utilized by masses of interns and incubator projects to develop concepts and solutions in the crisis areas of employment, housing, education, health care, transportation, mental health, disability culture, and voting.
Just round it up.

I’m just going to round it up and say– nothing about us without us, our clarion call, and next year I’m coming back. We’re going to ask for $15 million. The year after that $20, and the year after that $25. But MOPD has to forcefully act on behalf of the largest minority, not depend on other every agency in the city to do it. Thank you.
Thank you. Jordyn?

Hi. My name is Jordyn Rosenthal. I am a social worker. I am the Director of Advocacy at Community Access, a supportive housing

nonprofit. I’m a peer, a person with lived mental health experience, and I’m the lead organizer for Correct Crisis Intervention today which is about a coalition trying to have non-police mental health [inaudible] response systems. I just want to say thank you so much to all of the Chairs for staying here and listening to all the testimony. Power to you guys. I couldn’t do it. And I just– the things that I want to highlight that are in my testimony that are bulleted are the most important– or the most important things are. Last year, with help of the Progressive Caucus, we were able to get a $4.5 million investment in peer behavior health workforce. I want that up to $6 million, and I want the eligibility strengthened to only be things that are in the crisis continuum, whether it’s posts or pre or post or during, right? Specifically, Community Access where I work is asking for $540,000 of that $6 million and that’s to create interdisciplinary teams that we can have internally to our housing sites. And the other ask of this that's really relevant is– as the mayor announced the Office of Community Safety today, I really urge the council to hold a joint

oversight hearing between mental health and workforce development about peer behiavor workforce development. Because we need more peers and more community health workers to actually make OCS have teeth. With that, you can look at my testimony. Thank you.
Thank you. Dr. Recant, right?

I’m here actually on behalf of myself and other people who have suffered from being on accelerated outpatient treatment teams which I believe are illegal according to the Supreme Court decisions and federal law. Forced psychiatric commitment whether in-patient or out-patient is illegal. And the out-patient treatment teams are funded partly by the state and partly by the New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene, and if you’re going to give money to a– now, there are some people who may be dangerous, but Kathy Hochul just strengthened the law and made it very clear you don’t have to be dangerous. Anyone can commit you, and it has to be– but by law it has to be the least restrictive alternative. You’re given no

alternatives, and they kept me on there for 14 years. I called the person who wrote the law in Albany, and he told me all you have to do is tell them you don’t want it. No, it didn’t happen that way. And they keep you in your home. They don’t tell you when they’re coming. They abuse you when they come. They bang– they try to bang your door down and say if you don’t come right away we’re calling the police. They have called the police. And they– if you don’t take medicine and force medication according to a Supreme Court decision from a long time again, River City Cats [sic], it’s just not allowed unless it’s the only way to control very, very seriously violent behavior. They give it everyone, and they have the hearings every six months in the city– in the New York State– it’s called the ex parte room which means that you can’t be there, but the law says that the person receiving the treatment has to be part of the decision. And what’s wrong is that this is funded partly by the New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene. They’re going to fund such a program– it really needs to be changed, and the New York City– oh, okay.
No, round– just summarize it. Go ahead.
New York City Lawyers for the Public Health– Public Interest and the NYCLU and Legal Aid, they all oppose this law in many, many ways.
Alright. Thank you. Juan? Hi, Juan. How are you?

Hi. How are you? Thank you so much for the opportunity to testify. I’m Juan Pinzon. I’m the Senior Director of Government Relations at the Community Services Society. In my written testimony I lay out three things that New York City can do to for the access to health coverage. As federal changes, the HR1 bill, put thousands of New Yorkers at risk of losing of care. So, I’m going to highlight one of those things which is investing in trusted community-based programs like the Managed Care Consumer Assistance Program and Access Health NYC. Programs like MCCAP and Access Health are lifelines that connect New Yorkers through coverage, help them resolve insurance problems, ensure that they understand their rights. This

support is especially critical for immigrant communities at this time when fear and language barriers often prevent people from seeking help through government channels. The impact of MCCAP is clear. Since 2020, the program has handled more than 21,000 cases, secured over $1 million in savings for consumers and achieve a 90 percent success rate. The program is also reaching those most in need. Seven in ten clients are people of color and must speak a language other than English at home. Thanks for the Council investment last year, MCCAP expanded from 12 to 20 community-based organizations and that expansion is already working. We have seen nearly a 40 percent increase in cases in just the past few months, showing both a growing need and the programs affecting this. So, at this time when federal changes are creating confusion, fear, and new areas of coverage, this is exactly the kind of infrastructure that we need to protect. This is why we urge the Council to maintain MCCAP’s $2 million allocation in FY27 and to invest $4.5 million in Access Health NYC to support outreach and public education. Thank you.
Thank you. Before you go, there are questions by the other members. So, Chair Hanif?

Thank you, Chair, and thank you all for your testimony. I have questions for Robert, Elizabeth, and Mike. I’d love to know what your relationship has been with MOPD, the interface, and organizationally– personally or organizationally, and what you would like to see MOPD provide that they’re not providing right now, or what more do you want them to see.

Okay. So, my interaction with MOPD goes back to when I organized New York City’s first disability pride parade with Victor Calise [sp?], that then Commissioner, making it such an easy and wonderful event. It turned out very, very well. Thanks to him and– he was succeeded by someone who I never had communication with, except out in public. And I’m really delighted with the new Commissioner who had an early meeting with me. However, I believe that MOPD has always been underfunded and their funding has just gone down and down and down. And so now I believe it requires a

dramatic– I’ve always thought it required a dramatic increase to deal with the myriad problems that face our community. You know, we are, as I said, totally intersectional, but that means we have lots of– from mental health issues to mobility problems, to breathing problems. You know, I mean, we can’t have that interspersed through a bunch of different agencies dealt with by non-disabled people who just don’t get us. It really has to come under the auspices of one office which I’d have be a department really, but okay, all things in good time. Really would love to see MOPD better funded. It’ll be fully funded, as I said, after four years at $25 million. But compare that with all the other agencies. That’s not even comparable. So, we’re not asking for a lot. We’re asking for a big increase, but it’s not a lot of money in terms of what should be.
Thank you, Mike.
I think it can be a great agency and I look forward to your supporting our $10 million ask. Thank you.
Of course. Appreciate it. I’d like to hear from Robert and Elizabeth, if you have any comments.

Well, one of my earliest interactions with MOPD was watching them give these– their videos to teach me how to build an accessible website, and that’s– that really– yeah. That was a great thing and I think they could extend those kind of videos to younger students in the schools. It’d be a great thing, but remember, they need money. They need money. So, yeah, but that’s–
[interposing] Thank you.

My interaction with MOPD has been ever since I became an advocate for people with disabilities. And we need money just like we’re all here saying that everything’s underfunded for people with disabilities. You know, we’re the largest minority, but we are the least funded.
Thank you.

Chair Cabán has some questions, also.

CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Thank you. I just want to thank Dr. Recant for your testimony. Agree that there are a ton of problems with the laws around involuntary commitment and compulsive treatment, especially about how we define behavior. There’s a large disconnect between I think what mental health professionals, peers, doctors will define as dangerous and what others who are asked to go out into the community and enforce that law would define as dangerous. So, thank you for bringing light to that. Jordyn, I love that you brought up the workforce question. I know that I have reached out or we have reached out to the Committee on Economic Development, because I do want to hold a joint hearing on exactly that issue, not just a pipeline for peers, but also a pipeline for street workers. I think we’ve talked about this before, but not every professional has got the thing to do street work. You could be a social worker and say I want to do forensic social work, I want to do clinical social work, or I want to do work in our streets, and those are entirely different things. So, I want to thank you for that. I know we had the announcement on the

Office of Community Safety today, and from your perspective, just wanted to hear briefly what you think is going to be really key for being included in sort of like the organizational structure there.

Great question. Thank you so much, Council Member Cabán or Chairwoman Cabán. I would say the number one thing for me when I’m thinking about B-HEARD in terms of changes is not only structure of the teams of who is the responding, but upping the ratio of teams. I think if you look at the expansion of B-HEARD and the number of teams as it’s gone over like expanded to precincts, it hasn’t kept up pace. So, basically because there are so many eligible calls and not enough teams, even if we were to make it citywide or 24/7, we’d still come up against the same problems, because that ratio is so off. And with the fact of– circling back to hiring practices, there has been lots of discussion about the difficulty of hiring social workers for the B-HEARD teams, and my pitch to Council and Renita Francois [sp?] if she hears me is peers should replace the social worker on B-HEARD teams. You can have someone who is like me who holds both

identities. I am a social worker and a peer. And I’m just going to say, as Jordyn Rosenthal private citizen, I can say that my MSW education would not have primed me to do that street work of being a B-HEARD responder. I think that, you know, learning and peer work and a specific training that would need to be developed through H+H or now the Office of Community Safety would have to be developed to make this workforce. But being just a social worker doesn’t give you the check to have those skills. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Thank you so much, and thank you, Chair.

Thank you very much. This panel is dismissed. Thank you so much for being here and for testifying. Okay. So, the next panel will be Anna Kril, Laura Jean Hawkins, Rosa– okay, I’m going to butcher it, but anyway– James Bristo [sp?]. Anna, you want to go first?
Good afternoon.
Oh, you’re going to go first? Okay.

My name is Laura Jean Hawkins and I am the Advisory Board Chair of

Astoria, Queens SHAREing and CAREing, DBA SHAREing and CAREing. I am also a member of Elmhurst Hospital’s Community Advisory Board and Chair of the Patient Care Committee. I am here today as a woman who has been an advocate and ally of the cancer community for over 20 years. I am also a woman who has had her own health journey with thyroid disease and endometrial hyperplasia, undergoing years of biopsies and ultrasounds. Fortunately, all of my tests through the years have come back negative. That is not the case for many, however. There is currently a cancer epidemic in our state, our country and our city. Cancer is occurring in younger and younger adults. These are called early onset cancers which are diagnosed in adults between the ages of 18 and 49. A very public example of this is the recent death of actor James Van Der Beek who died of stage three colon cancer in February, just one month before his 49th birthday. No one knows why this is happening, but what I can tell you is that more and more people in our community are being diagnosed with cancer and they are turning to us for help, help that is getting harder and harder to do with our limited

funds. Since 2020, we have experienced a 25 percent increase in the demand for our services. Funding under the Council’s Cancer Services Initiative has stayed flat since the initiative was created. The time for increased funding is now. On behalf of my board, I thank you for the Council’s many years of support and for your funding. You’ve been very generous, but now is the time that we ask you to please increase funding for the Cancer Services Initiative and support our request of $250,000. Every dollar increased is a life benefitted and possibly saved. Thank you.
Thank you. Rosa?

Good afternoon. My name is Rosa Sarmiento and I am one of the SHAREing and CAREing’s bilingual Spanish navigators. I’m also the wife of a cancer survivor, a Community Advisory Board member at Elmhurst Hospital. As a patient navigator I have focused on increasing SHAREing and CAREing community outreach efforts in my community, the Spanish-speaking community through Queens, educating them about cancer awareness and the importance of yearly and timely cancer screening. As an immigrant

myself, I understand the fears the new arrivals to our city may experience. At SHAREing and CAREing we have to strive to build trust, reduce fear, and eliminate cultural and financial barriers in order to promote early detection and treatment, as well as to improve access to life-saving services. Over the past two years, I have assisted many Spanish-speaking survivors, helping them to apply for public benefits, secure access right, and other transportation services, and I have authorized emerging needs assistance for medical bills, rent, utilities, and food. My team and I have also gone out into the community educating vulnerable at-risk population and encourage cancer screening, and the more that we do, the more that is the need. Since 2020, the demand for our services have increased 25 percent. Our funding from the Council, however, has stayed flat. On behalf of the Queens cancer community survivors across the city, I urge you to support our request for increased funding. Thank you.
Thank you. Anna?

Good afternoon. My name is Anna Kril. I am a two-time breast cancer survivor and

Founder and President of SHAREing and CAREing. It brings to mind 33 years ago when I was initially diagnosed with breast cancer. I pray to God to grant me life, because I wanted to raise my two little girls. With that prayer also came my commitment that I would give back every single day. From that point on, that’s how SHAREing and CAREing was created. We address the disparities in Queens County. We provide support services for those who are newly diagnosed and in treatment. We help people in every single aspect of their road with cancer. We are the face of hope. We’re the face of survivorship, and we are their life link. So, with that, I have to say in 2020, again, I was diagnosed with breast cancer, and during my treatment process, I also realized a very alarming fact. Younger and younger people are being diagnosed. Their needs are greater and greater. And we need your help in order to be able to help them survive. On behalf of the cancer community, I truly urge you, please support our funding request of $250,000. It will mean everything to those who are struggling with this horrific disease. Thank you for your time and your support.
Thank you. James?

Good afternoon, Chair Schulman, Chair Cabán, Chair Hanif, and members of the committees. I’m James Bristow, Vice President of Public Policy and Government Affairs for Vibrant Emotional Health. Thank you for the opportunity to testify today. Vibrant is widely recognized as a national leader in crisis response. As the administrator of the 988 suicide and crisis lifeline, we oversee and strengthen a nationwide network providing life-saving support 24 hours a day, seven days a week. At the same time, we operate NYC 988 locally, giving us both macro and micro level insight into suicide preventino operations. Beyond crisis response, Vibrant Emotional Health has spent decades building deep trust in communities across the five boroughs and pioneering New York City’s first family support program in 1989, to managing one of the city’s most robust youth and family peer support networks. We’ve consistently led with innovation, compassion, and cultural humility. Our programs serve New Yorkers from all walks of life, including youth and young adults, families navigating complex

systems, older adults seeking to remain in community, and individuals living with co-occurring challenges. Turning to the fiscal year 27 Preliminary Budget. It is encouraging to see an attempt being made to address structural programmatic deficits, particularly as it pertains to right-sizing the out year budgets for supportive housing early intervention. It is also positive to see investment in the new public health lab, as well as the much needed cost of living adjustment. Additionally, Vibrant Emotional Health greatly appreciates the Council administration’s current support for NYC 988 operations due to provision of an additional $5 million in Fiscal Year 26 which was added in the adopted budget and is implemented via council discretionary dollars. This additional funding facilitates increased capacity for NYC 988. The criticality of this funding has only resumed the past year as contact volume has continued to go up year after year, and the additional support allowed us to reduce wait times for all New York City contacts, ensuring quicker access to a trained crisis counselor for health seekers. We are confident the Council and

the administration’s ability to see the continuation of this vital funding stream into Fiscal Year 27. Furthermore, we are optimistic about the administration and council’s commitment to mental health and want to point out additional areas that are ripe for enhanced investment. For example, youth peer services are an important tool in reducing barriers in mental health care. Yeah, just one more sentence.
Summarize.

Yeah. Young people today face unprecedented mental health challenges. Research consistently demonstrates that youth are more likely to open up to peers who share similar life experiences and speak their language, targeting investment towards robust youth peer services such as a help line as a way to see instant benefit. Thank you.

Okay. So, wait, before you go, Chair Cabán has some questions and Chair Hanif. So, Chair Cabán?

CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Great. Should we expect an increase in the cost of administering the 988 system in future years?

Well, the contact volume continues to go up year over year. So, I would say there is going to be eventually– there’s going to be a need for additional funding to maintain pace and to be able to ensure we have the appropriate capacity to address all help-seekers that contact us. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: And in April 2025, Gothamist reported discrepancies between how Vibrant Emotional Health and the city– sorry– and the city– thank you– calculate 988 calls and contact volume, and these are discrepancies that appear to have contributed to a reduction in city funding for the 988 help line program. Can you clarify the nature of these discrepancies? WEre you able to hear the front part of my question?
Yes. You’re talking about– CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: [interposing] Okay, great.
discrepancies in data reporting? CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Yes.

I mean, yeah. So, I’m happy to say that the– you know, our contract with DOHMH has been right-sized since then, and so it’s, you know, at a level along with the other sources of funding including the Council discretionary dollars to where we’re able to, you know, meet capacity this time. Though, it is important to see that funding continued. You’ll have to forgive me, I did just start less than two months ago with Vibrant, and so I’m happy to follow up with you with more specific details. But my understanding is that the discrepancy related to how metrics were tracked as it related to health-seekers who also were then referred to peer specialists and also to mobile crisis teams and how those were counted in the overall tally, and I know we had a series of meetings with DOHMH to reconcile that data and to be on the same page. So, you know, going forward I think we’re very much in line, and like I said before, we were able to address

the previous kind of contractual issues that had arisen. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Yeah. And then actually going to the contract itself, what portion of the operations are not fully covered by city or state funding, and then how are you current– like, how are the other costs being absorbed?
Are you including discretionary dollars in the city funding? CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Maybe split it up and–
Well, I would– I mean, I can get you the exact breakdown. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Yeah.

The– I mean, the city and state funding, some of that is passed through from the federal government, that encompasses the whole NYC 988 operations. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Okay. So, there is currently not costs that are being absorbed by outside funding, non-governmental funding?

Not to my knowledge, but I will get back to you on that.

CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Yeah, and then if you could follow up with the breakdown on the federal, state, city funding–

[interposing] Yep. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: that would be great. And then my last question for you. What are your current staffing turnover rates within 988 operations? LIke to what extent are compensation levels tied to available funding affecting your ability to recruit, to retain qualified counselors.

I appreciate that question. Thank you. I mean retention and recruitment is always an issue, and you know, the more you're able to provide as compensation, it enhances both of those aspects. We have been able to hire up pretty aggressively in the recent years, but we do see a need to increase the salary floor to be able to maintain– to retain our staff. So, that's something that we would like to discuss further with you and– CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: What’s the counselor get paid?

Say that again?

CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: What does a counselor get paid?
Let me follow up with you on that. I don’t want to mispeak. I’m sorry. I don’t have that in front of me. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Great. Thank you. THanks, Chair.
Okay. Chair Hanif.
Thank you. I wanted to know from the panel if you’ve had interactions through your organization with MOPD, and if so what kind of interaction have you had?
We haven’t.

Got it. And you know, everything that was described in your testimonies– and thank you so much for sharing your story. It takes a lot of courage to not just heal from the pain, but then to get up every single day wanting to do this work for the rest of us and for generations to come. So, thank you. Breast cancer, some of the mental health issues that 988 responds to certainly include short-term or long-term disabilities. So,

I’m curious which city agencies you've interacted with the most? As far as agencies– CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: [interposing] Or offices.
with the offices, we basically work very closely with our public hospitals in Queens county. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Okay.

So, that's who we primarily deal with. I have not dealt with other agencies other than perhaps Rosa who deals with getting, you know, services for the individuals that may qualify for let’s say food stamps or other services, assess–A-Ride or even public assistance. I mean, she’s better qualified to answer the questions, but she deals with those agencies. So, if you– CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: [interposing] Got It.

And I will just say of course the Department of Health administers our contracts. So we work closely with them, but vis a vis our contract.

CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Okay. And then so, is it right to say that if someone you know is basically long-term disabled and will have to take off from work, that you all are primarily working with your public hospital in Queens?

Well, with the hospital and also with processing or helping them process their disability papers, you know, working through what they require in order to be entitled to the benefits that they should be getting. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: And how much of– how many, like, cancer patients are disabled in terms of unable to work after diagnosis?

Alright. I could mention to you with the younger population that I’ve recently been working with. Most of them need to be not working while they’re in treatments, because the treatments are really quite aggressive. So it limits their ability to work. Possibly, they may be able to work remotely. It depends on their employer, again. So, I would say many of our younger ones are the ones who have to go on whether it be short-term or long-term disability. And unfortunately, with the

young ones, their cancer recurs. No sooner did they– let’s say it’s breast cancer. No sooner do they have a diagnosis of breast cancer and finish that treatment, within six months all of a sudden now it went to the bones or it went to the colon. So, their road is a continual unfortunately. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Thanks for sharing that. That’s terrible, but good to know. And you’re not asking for a lot of money.

Thank you. Thank you to– panel is dismissed. Thank you. Okay, next panel: Casey Starr [sp?], Fiona O’Grady [sp?], Kamari Cruz [sp?], Laura Savino, Omar Cao [sp?], and Bill Gross. Okay, Bill is here, okay. Faith Baham [sp?], Jihoon Kim, Deirdre De Leo, and Doctor David Appel [sp?]. Geordana Weber and Maryam Mohammad-Miller, or Maryam, I’m sorry, misread it. Omar Cao? Alright, why don’t you start– we’ll start from the left.

Chair Schulman, Cabán, Hanif, and members of the Council, thank you for the opportunity to testify. My name is Jihoon Kim. I serve as President and CEO of InUnity Alliance. I’m also a social worker and peer professional by

training and a person in long-term recovery for co-occurring substance use and mental health disorders. It’s an honor to be here today representing 150 substance use and mental health providers. In addition to advocacy, we provide training and serve as the exclusive certifying body for peer recovery credentialing in New York. Our members formed InUnity Alliance to strengthened, coordinated person-centered care while preserving the specialized expertise of each service system. Substance use disorders and mental health conditions remain leading contributors to disability and preventable death. They’re also closely tied to housing instability, child welfare involvement and legal system contact. Structural pressures of reducing capacity and delaying access to care when early intervention is most protective and cost effective. Rates do not cover the actual cost of delivering services and unpredictable grant payments make it difficult for programs to plan and operate with stability. New York City cannot reduce crises including homelessness without addressing the conditions that limit the capacity of community-based

services designed to prevent them. We urge you to implement the $15.5 million IMT expansion investment including the Step Down Program which was included in the budget last year, invest $65.3 million in supportive housing to preserve existing units, continue to fund a three percent COLA for human services workers, and provide increased funding for New York City Council’s substance use disorder and mental health initiatives as included in our written testimony. Lastly, vocational treatment services have seen a sharp increase in referrals from HRA due to work requirements for SNAP and soon for Medicaid. An assessment of need with funding to support the increase in service recipients is necessary to sustain these programs. Thank you to the New York City Council for championing these life-saving initiatives. I appreciate the committee’s time and consideration of these requests.
Thank you. Next.

Good afternoon, Chairs Cabán, Schulman, Hanif, and members of the committee. Thank you for having me and your leadership in strengthening health services in New York. I’m

Deirdre De Leo, Director of Behavioral Health Crisis and Assessment Programs at VNS Health. For over 130 years our teams have helped New Yorkers live, age and heal in their homes and communities. Today, we serve more than 95,000 people across the city, older adults, people living with serious mental illness, and people with physical disabilities. To reduce crises and improve safety, we need strong sustained investment in community-based behavioral health care and in the partnerships that make this work possible. We see the impact of these partnerships daily. During the recent code blue emergency our teams worked alongside DOHMH to help people get to shelter and services during dangerous winter conditions. This same kind of work, our Mobile Crisis ACT and IMT teams do year round, meeting people right in their neighborhoods responding to crises and helping them stay connected to care and housing. But crisis response alone isn’t enough. Reaching people earlier makes a tremendous difference. With support from City Council discretionary funds, our Older Adult Mental Health initiative brings primary care directly into people’s homes. One couple we worked with

struggling with isolation and depression told us, please keep checking up on us. What you do may seem small, but it’s not small to us. We see the same impact with young people. Through the Council-supported Promise Zone program we provide counseling in schools so challenges don’t become crises. As the city continues its behavioral health efforts and the new Office of Community Safety, we have a real opportunity to build on programs that are already working, centering the voices and experiences of frontline clinicians will be essential as we move forward. Thank you again for supporting our Older Adult Mental Health Initiative and Promise Zone programs which help New Yorkers get care before crisis occurs.
Thank you. Next.

Good afternoon, Chairs and members of the Council. My name is Bill Gross. I serve as the Chief Services Officer at SAGE which is the nation’s largest and oldest organization dedicated to improving the lives of LGBTQ+ older adults. Since our founding in 1978, SAGE has worked tirelessly to advocate for policies and programs that

empower LGBTQ+ elders, ensuring that they can age with dignity and security and support. The people that SAGE serves have unique and often complex health care issues. For example, approximately 14 percent of LGBTQ+ New Yorkers over age 50 report frequent poor physical health. Many of our constituents [sic] delay or avoid seeking care in mainstream settings since LGBTQ+ adults are twice as likely as their non-LGBTQ+ counterparts to report experiencing discrimination from a health care provider. In addition as of 2024, 56 percent of all New Yorkers living with HIV are age 50 or over, and nearly one in six new HIV diagnoses occur within this age group. Our SAGE Center Network serves as a safety net for LGBTQ+ elders and older elders living with HIV. We connect them to affirming providers and we provide programming that reduces isolation, improves access to services by offering benefits counseling, legal and financial planning, educational workshops, health and wellness programs, support groups, and nutritional meals. These vital services are made possible from our partnership with the New York City Council. Our top priority is maintaining our

funding, ensuring that LGBTQ+ older adults can live with dignity and to call the city home.
Thank you very much. Next.

Thank you, Committee Chairs Cabán, Hanif and Schulman, for holding this budget hearing which recognizes the critical issue of supporting the health of New Yorkers. My name is Geordana Weber and I’m Chief Program Officer of Service Program for Older People, or SPOP. We are the only agency in New York City that is exclusively dedicated to community-based mental health care for older adults, and we provide outpatient treatment to 1,000 adults each year. We’ve been doing this work for over 45 years, and we offer services via telehealth, at our offices on the upper west side of Manhattan and at satellite locations in Brooklyn, the Bronx and Manhattan. We’re only as strong as our network of community partners and we’re grateful for the opportunity to work with dozens of hospitals, older adult centers, and aging service providers to reach out to isolated adults who would otherwise have

no access to mental health care. Older adults represent the fastest growing segment of New York City’s population, and they are generally older, more diverse, and more isolated than ever before. An estimated 20 percent of the population will experience a mental health challenge at some point, ranging from mild depression to serious mental illness such as schizophrenia or bipolar disorder which can interfere with their ability to function and live independently, and life can be very difficult for an older adult who’s managing physical and behavioral health challenges. Our role at SPOP is to provide mental health services that reduce symptoms, teach coping and problem-solving skills, and support social interaction so that older adults can stay in their communities. We’re especially focused on the needs of older adults with serious mental illness. Most SMI mental health care programs are designed for younger adults and don’t support clients who are also managing cognitive changes, fragile health, and the practical realities of later life. Aging services, meanwhile, are often not equipped to provide robust psychiatric care. Older

adults with SMI fall through the cracks until they surface in the most visible and expensive systems we have, emergency rooms, hospitals, shelters, and too often the justice system. I’ll wrap up. I therefore urge the committee to advocate for robust funding for programs and services to support community-based, age-affirming mental health care for older adults with serious mental illness. Thanks so much.
Thank you. Next.

Good afternoon. My name is Doctor David Appel and I’m the Coordinator of the New York City School-based Health Alliance. I’d like to thank the Committee Chair Schulman and members of New York City Council’s Health Committees for the opportunity to submit testimony on school-based health centers. In my opinion, without baseline funding, the financial viability of New York City’s 139 school-based health centers are in jeopardy. Increased staffing costs, decreased school enrollment, and newly migrated children with fewer options and significant unmet needs all contribute to placing school-based health centers in financial jeopardy. School-based health centers are being

forced to cut back a range of services and significant number of school-based health centers around the city have closed being replaced by contract nurses at a cost similar to what we are asking to keep New York City school-based health centers in place, and it contributes to increased long-term health care costs, higher teen pregnancy rates, and lower graduation rates, raised levels of unrelated mental health issues, and drives up ER use and hospitalizations for asthma. I’m here today to urge City Council to use Tax Levy dollars to support school-based health centers at the level of $100,000 per campus and $100 per student. Through the New York State Department of Health Article 6 enhancement, there’s a 20 percent match to New York City funding for school-based health centers. So the cost is less than that for a school nurse. School-based health centers are very efficient way to spend Tax Levy dollars. And I included in my testimony a comparison of services of a school of 2,000 children. It would take two school nurses at a cost of approximately $300,000, and they provide first aid care, can do medication administration.

School-based health centers provide mental health services, dental care, vision care, thousands of immunizations a year, reproductive health, and well child–
[interposing] Thank you very much. Next.

Good afternoon. My name is Laura Savino. I am the Senior Vice President of Care Management for Institute for Community Living. ICL helps the city address the most serious mental illness crisis by supporting more than 10,000 New Yorkers annually, including housing 4,000 people each night. We successfully support individuals with the most significant problems, and these are people that you might have encountered on the subway or the streets through programs like IMT, Intense Mobile Treatment. IMT works because it provides long-term comprehensive services and is rooted in the community. It helps people stabilize, remain housed, and avoid costly traumatic system cycling. Today, nearly 700 New Yorkers sit on an IMT wait list. Individuals, again, cycling through shelters, emergency rooms, incarceration while we know that

there is a model that works. There are simply not enough IMT slots, and we are letting people stay on IMT longer than necessary because clients who have stabilized on IMT have no structured bridge to lower levels of care. This is why ICL launched STEPS. This is our Step-down Treatment to Ensure Personal Success which is a recovery-oriented pilot designed to provide structure, lower touch, less intensive traditional support services to help free up these critical IMT spots or slots– I’m sorry. Since launching STEPS in 2023, we’ve served over 150 clients. Of the 73 enrolled, 97 percent of those were housed, 89 percent avoided hospitalization, 86 percent avoided ER visits, and 100 percent were not arrested or incarcerated. STEPS is also a fraction of the price or of the cost of IMT. Now, the Council recognized this and allocated $4.5 million specifically for STEPS, yet this money has not yet been procured. We are urging the release of these funds, and we are also urging you to hold, please, joint oversight hearing with the Committee for Mental Health, Addiction, Disabilities and a committee on workshop development for the topic of behavioral

workforce development in which is especially pertinent to Mayor Mamdani’s promotion with his vision for the Department of Community Safety. If we don’t allow these funds to be released, over 100 New Yorkers potentially have nowhere to go back into the community, and they could potentially land back on the streets with no care and no services.
Okay. Thank you. Next.

Good afternoon. My name is Maryam Mohammed-Miller and I’m the Director of Government Relations and Policy at Planned Parenthood of Greater New York or PPGNY for short. I would like to thank the Committee Chairs, Council Member Schulman, Cabán, and Hanif, for the opportunity for PPGNY to discuss our programs and services. PPGNY has been a trusted provider of sexual reproductive health care and education programs throughout New York City for over 100 years. In 2025 we conducted over 67,000 patient visits and engaged over 20,000 individuals through our education and community engagement programs. We provide the full range of sexual reproductive health care

services at our health care centers. We are deeply committed to providing care no matter what, and we’re thankful for the Council’s continuous support of our work to ensure New Yorkers access the care they deserve. We also have faced a series of attacks from the federal administration and politicians hostile to sexual reproductive health care, limiting our ability to provide the care New Yorkers rely on. So, that is why today we are asking the Council to continue to support the work we do, but asking for increases in several initiatives including the Reproductive and SExual Health Initiative that supports our clinical service work and our education programs, specifically our youth health promoters program that engages young people to access the care that they deserve and empowers their ability to navigate health care services. We’re also asking for an increase in the New York City Abortion Access Fund which is the first in the nation Abortion Access Fund that the Council proudly championed to ensure New Yorkers can get abortion care. We’re also asking for an increase in a dedicated contraceptive fund to support our ability to provide long-acting reversible contraceptive care

to New Yorkers in need, as well as an increase in the Trans Equity Program initiative to support LGBTQ New Yorkers in need of gender-affirming care throughout our city. We look forward to continue to work with the Council to support this work, make sure that New Yorkers can affordable and quality health care. Thank you.
Thank you so much. I want to– any questions for the panel?
Yes.
Go ahead.

I would also like to know if your organizations have had interactions with MOPD? I’m just trying to understand given the intersection of disability and all of your testimonies, just how MOPD might be playing a role in the work that you’re doing. What do you think of when we say the mayor’s got an Office of Disability– for people with disabilities?

I can go. SPOC would love to work with MOPD. We– one of the things the Commissioner said earlier on about how– when you make spaces disability-friendly, you’re also making

them aging-friendly, not to mention family-friendly. I think there’s a lot of opportunity for cross-over. At SPOC we work a lot with people who are blind and visually impaired. We have a satellite at Visions, at Cellas [sic] Manor, and we’ve not worked directly with MOPD, but we have agencies that are referring to us like Visions or like the Lighthouse come and do trainings with our staff so that we are as disability-affirming as we can be. Understandably, that’s only just one type of disability.
Thank you.

Yeah, Planned Parenthood of Greater New York would love the opportunity to work with MOPD. We have launched a series of programs targeting folks with intellectual disabilities, young people specifically in the school system, creating specific programs to provide comprehensive sexual education in ways that meet their educational and IDD needs. So, that program has been funded by private donors, supporters of Planned Parenthood, but would love to, you know, concrete a partnership with the City to make sure that those resources are still available to folks,

especially given funding cuts that we’re seeing for education– from the Trump administration to be frank.
What’s the funding associated with this program?

We’ve gotten private donations. I know that there’s some state grant dollars. Not clear on city-level funding, but we’ve, you know, inquired and would love some clarity on what the pathways are to fund that program.
Got it. Thank you.

Thank you. This panel’s dismissed. Thank you. Thank you very much. Okay, next panel: Allie Taylor, Candice Kumai-- if I’m pronouncing– hopefully I’m pronouncing that correctly– Meagan Licari, Laura MacAvoy, Kathleen Raab, and Chelsea Domaleski [sp?]. Go ahead, Allie, go for it.

My name is Allie Taylor, President of Voters for Animal Rights. In last year’s budget for the first time ever, the city allocated a half million dollars for spay/neuter services to Flatbush Cats which funded approximately 3,500 surgeries. 2,200 if those surgeries have been

completed so far, and they are on target to complete the rest by the end of this June. There is no question that Flatbush Cats’ program has been a success for the pet parents and rescuers who received these affordable services. However, this investment represents only a small fraction of what is really needed. The number of requests that Flatbush Cats receives for spay/neuter surgeries and wellness appointments far outpaces available spots. Those 3,500 surgeries account for roughly two percent of the estimated need. To effectively address the 500,000 stray cats on our streets and reduce shelter intake of owned pets at NYC ACC, the city must fund nearly 190,000 spay/neuter surgeries annually. Without scaling these services, we will continue to fall behind. Flatbush Cats has the infrastructure to scale up, but they need far more city funding to provide more surgeries and wellness appointments. That’s why we’re urging the Council to allocate $1.5 million in this year’s budget for spay/neuter. The rescue community is stretched beyond capacity. Volunteers across the city are stepping in to do this work, often using their own time and money and

resources and this is not a sustainable system. We can’t continue to rely on informal unpaid workforce to provide what is essentially a critical municipal service. In addition to spay/neuter, I want to highlight another urgent issue, pet food insecurity. Lst yer’s budget included zero funding for pet food pantries despite the growing need. Financial hardship remains one of the leading reasons people surrender their pets. Right now, families are being forced to make impossible choices between feed themselves and feeding their pets. In speaking with human food pantries such as New York Common Pantry, we know that pet food is one of the most frequently requested groceries with the least availability. By providing funding for pet food to existing human pantries, they can provide warehouse and distribute pet food most efficiently. We are calling for $2 million in funding for pet food pantry programs. And in summary, we urge the Council to build on last year’s progress by allocating $1.5 million for spay neuter and $2 million for pet food pantries. The cost of providing spay/neuter and pet food is one-third the cost of what it would cost to shelter

an animal at NYC ACC, and by investing in spay/neuter and pet food pantries, the city can take meaningful proactive steps to reduce shelter intake, improve public health, and support working families. These are not just animal welfare issues–
[interposing] Okay, we– we have to–
Sorry.
That’s alright. No worries. Next?

Thank you so much, Council Members for listening, and Council Member Lynn Schulman, it’s great to see you again, and Chair Cabán and Chair Hanif, thank you for listening. I’m Candice Kumai. I am a journalist and writer here in New York City, and I’m one of the hundreds if not thousands of volunteers that goes out onto the streets every week to find cats in need, and sometimes dogs as well. We go out alone to rescue these animals in distress, and because I’m not a city worker I get heckled by locals or sometimes harassed, and I’m put in dangerous situations in the Bronx and in Harlem when I’m just out trying to help our cats

and dogs. For those of us who step in, we are faced with a multitude of challenges. We care deeply but we are exhausted. Emotionally, we are also suffering just as much as the cats and dogs on the streets. But with proper investment in spay and neuter services and programs like this pet pantry that we speak about. We can change this. Every single week I talk to different members. We’re all volunteers completely out-of-pocket, and the common thread that we all share is that are tired and we are exhausted and we are completely out of pocket emotionally and financially. New York State motto is Excelsior which means ever upward. This is a promise to strive for a better future. New York has always been an example that the world has watched, and I please urge you today to put money towards these initiatives for the pets of New York, and I ask you, we should be striving together for excelsior today. Thank you so much for your time.
Thank you. Next?

Good afternoon. My name is Meagan Licari and I’m the Executive Director of Puppy Kitty New York City. As most of you know, the

city is facing a quiet crisis, one that lives in our alley ways, under our stoops, in the homes of families struggling to keep up. The overpopulation crisis is not just an animal issue, it’s a community issue and it requires real city support. Low-cost, city-funded spay and neuter is most humane and effective way to reduce suffering on our streets. It works. It stabilizes colonies, prevents endless litters and improves neighborhood health. But right now, this burden is falling entirely on small rescuers just like all of us up here, volunteers and other everyday New Yorkers. That is not sustainable. Our organization alone rescued over 800 animals last year, and every one was spayed or neutered through public funds through donations that we have to raise. But for every one that we help, many, many more are turned away due to lack of reseoruces. At the same time, our food bank is overwhelmed. We currently serve about 45 private rescue groups and cannot expand to the general public despite the growing need. Families are being forced to choose between feeding themselves or their pets, paying rent versus veterinary care. When access to food and vet care

disappears, the consequences ripple, more unaltered animals, more litter, and more strain on the shelters and rescue groups. If we want to solve the overpopulation, we must address the root causes, and that means investing in spay and neuter and supporting community food banks. Prevention is more humane and far more cost-effective. That’s why we are asking you to please award $1.5 million for spay/neuter and $2 million for food banks. We are already doing the work. We just need the city to stand with us. Thank you.
Thank you. Next?

Hi. My name is Laura MacAvoy. I’m the Secretary of the Board and a long-time volunteer for Puppy Kitty New York City. I’m here today asking for support for the funding of spay/neuter and the pet food pantry programs for the fiscal budget of whatever year we’re in now. Who knows. We’re struggling against massive endless tide of suffering, doing our best to meet the needs of our city’s animals and people, but there’s only so much we can do as individual organizations. This issue will take organized systemic change with city support

for spay/neuter, for rescues and owned pets, and for pet food pantries to help keep families together. On a national scale, 5.8 million cats and dogs entered shelters and rescued as reported to shelter animals count by the 13,471 participating organizations in 2025. Of those, 9,371 organizations are rescues without a government contract which accounts for 69.5 percent of reporting agencies. According to a 2025 survey published in Pet Food Industry, Volume 67, issue four, 42 percent of respondents in middle-income brackets of pet owners which would be a household income of $60-99,000 annually reported significant challenges due to the high cost of pet food, and 46 percent of pet owners in the lower to modest income households reported significant challenges. Funding for pet food pantries would help alleviate some of this burden for New Yorkers, and we do have the infrastructure to run a pet food pantry, we just don’t have the funding to support individuals. On a smaller anecdotal scale, just this month we’ve done intake for 11 cats abandoned in carriers outside. One was on our porch directly overnight at 5:00 a.m., and 10 were left in Pet Co.

adoption center partners, including a litter of six kittens.
Just summarize.
We need help. Thank you.
Thank you.

Hello. My name is Chelsea Domaleski [sp?]. I currently work with several organizations across New York City including New York Common Pantry, the Campaign Against Hunger, and Paws New York to provide pet food and essential supplies to vulnerable residents. Every day, New Yorkers face an impossible choice, feed themselves or feed the pet they love like family. It’s happening now. We have senior clients right now who are skipping their own Meals on Wheels donations to feed their dogs and cats. At ACC there’s thousands of animals entering the shelter every year due to owner surrender with a significant portion driven by preventable financial hardship, including food insecurity, lack of access to veterinary care, and housing instability. These surrenders disproportionately affect marginalized communities already burdened by systemic inequalities. We can

change this. Investing in shelter prevention initiatives, low and no-cost veterinary services, including spay and neuter and pet pantries, keep families together and reduces strain on the shelter system. We can put funding where it matters most, food, medical care, and essential supplies. These are simple, cost-effective interventions. When families can rely on consistent access to pet food, they no longer have to stretch already limited budgets or go without eating themselves. It’s one less burden, one more reason they can stay stable and keep their companions by their side. Pets are not a luxury. They’re a family emotional support and often a lifeline. Keeping them out of shelters and with the people who love them is not only humane, it is fiscally responsible and socially just. I urge you to fund these preventative solutions, because no one in New York City should have to surrender a beloved pet just to survive. Right now, at the Campaign against Hunger, we have a 2,500 person waiting list for pet food and supplies. This is already something that we have in motion where we’re working alongside human pantries. It does not require any kind of

infrastructure intervention. It does not require building new buildings or hiring new workers. It just requires a budget so that we can allocate food and resources to our human pantry partners to serve the people who every single day are trying to feed themselves and stay afloat in New York City and it’s something that the mayor’s office can do. Thank you for your time.
Thank you. Next?

Good afternoon members of the Council. Thank you for this opportunity to speak on behalf of SPCA International about the issue that directly impacts animal welfare, public health and the stability of families across New York City. Every day, animals are born into situations where there are not enough homes, there are not enough resources, and there’s not enough support systems to care for them. The result is predictable, overcrowded shelters, increased strain on municipal services, and unnecessary suffering for animals. We know how to prevent this. Spaying and neutering is the single most-effective humane solution to reducing pet overpopulation. It decreases intake pressure on

shelters, improves animal health outcomes and reduces long-term costs for our city. This work is not about limiting life, it is about protecting it. The prevention is not enough. As both a representative for SPCA International and a New York City pet owner, I know how quickly the cost of care can become overwhelming. For many families, access to affordable pet food through community pet food pantries can make the difference between keeping a beloved pet or losing them. Pet food pantries are a critical low-cost intervention that stabilizes households, prevents unnecessary surrenders and allows people to care for the animals they love. The resources also support the network of rescuers and community caregivers who are already doing this work, often with limited support. Without access to affordable sterilization services and pet food, their ability to respond is severely constrained. Funding accessible trap/neuter/return programs and pet food pantries is not just an animal welfare decision, it is a public investment, a smart public investment. It reduces suffering, prevents unnecessary surrenders and strengthens our communities. We are not asking

the Council to take on a new problem, we’re asking you to invest in solutions that already work. Together–
[interposing] [inaudible] Oh.
Together we can break the cycle of overpopulation and we can keep families and their pets together. Thank you so much for your time and consideration.

Thank you. And I just want to state for the record that I spearheaded the pilot program for the $500,000 last year for the spay/neuter. I am an advocate for it. I’m pushing for it myself this year, and also for the pantries. So, I’m pushing on both of those scores [sic].
Thank you.

Just so that you– just so everybody knows. So, we’ll see where we wind up, but thank you so much. Panel is dismissed. Thank you. Okay. Ronni Marks, Jeanine Gurega [sp?], Robert Dezrelo [sp?]-- sorry if I mispronounce that– Elaine Lepena [sp?], and Wen– Parisome [sp?]. Wen doesn’t need a last name? Okay. Alright, so who do

we have? We have Ronnie. We have Wen. I’m sorry? Okay. He’s not here. We’re going to call up Hadley Weiss [sp?], Charles De San Pedro, Jr., and Blanca Simmons [sp?]. Okay. You go first. Whoever wants to go first? Jeanine?
She’s going to talk for Robert. He had to leave.
Okay, fine.

Thank you for the opportunity to speak to you today. I want to thank Chair Schulman, Council Member Cabán and other Council Members and staff for supporting the hepatitis community in the past. I am here today as a representative of the Hepatitis C Mentoring Support Group. I have been working for 12 years on the ground and with the underserved communities providing training on education and supportive services within syringe exchange programs and drop-in centers. I work closely with the founder and Executive Director of ACMSG [sic] Ronnie Marks, who in addition to being a patient has experienced working with both patients and providers. Educational groups and supportive patient mentoring services have been shown to be

important elements of successful and cost-effective medical care for patients with hepatitis C and other chronic health conditions. The services improve the quality of life as well as medical outcomes for patients. The training ACMSG provides for health care providers help them to have a better understanding of how to work with all patients with an emphasis on high-risk populations such as people with substance use disorder, those co-infected with HIV, LGBTQ community, youth and women of child-bearing age dealing with hepatitis C. Our hope is to see this provider model for the entire country with New York City as the first city to eliminate hepatitis C. We need increased services for hepatitis, peer navigators, harm reduction, and syringe exchange services. This is why it is critical that we reduce missed opportunities to screen and diagnose patients who seek care in emergency rooms and hospitals, as well as educating providers and staff on the stigma faced by people who use drugs. There are opportunities to move towards elimination by increasing the focus on treating patients who are in the hospital for extended periods

of time. Education is needed in overdose prevention, hepatitis and HIV. People need to understand this endemic connection between substance use and infectious disease. As an educator in the field and someone who has witnessed the lack of knowledge in communities, I can–
[interposing] So, just wrap it up. That’s Robert’s testimony?
Yeah.
Yeah. And then I’m going to give you two minutes for yours. So wrap his up.
Okay. So, please help us ensure that all New York City residents have access to hepatitis C testing, treatment and care regardless of race, gender and economic status. Thank you.
Okay. Then you will have two minutes on your own?
Right, I’m going to go.
You’re going to go first?
Yeah. I’m not going to read this whole thing. I’m just–
[interposing] Two minutes, Ronni.

Okay, okay. Thank you for the support that you have given us. I am a patient who cured of hepatitis C and my mission is to see and give the opportunity to others to have that no matter who they are or where they come from. The Health Department estimates that 330,000 people are living with hepatitis B and C, and without care and treatment, this can lead to progress to serious liver disease, liver cancer and even death. As a patient who has been cured, I can tell you what a difference it makes in your life. I’ve seen people turn their lives around from being cured, and it gives them opportunities for other ways in their life to improve. Continued increased support of the viral hepatitis initiative is vital to the health and wellness of New York’s most vulnerable. We have the infrastructure. We need more funding to expand these services. Please help us ensure that all New York residents have access to hepatitis C education, testing, treatment and care regardless of race,

gender or economic status. Let’s make New York City the first city to eliminate hepatitis.
Thank you. Jeannine, go ahead.

To Chairperson Schulman and members of the Committee on Health, my name is Jeannine Garriga and I work with the Hepatitis C Mentor and Support Group where I focus on hepatitis C education, training and community engagement as part of the New York City viral hepatitis prevention initiative. Nearly 330,000 New Yorkers are living with chronic hepatitis B or C, and without care and treatment many will progress to serious liver disease, liver cancer or even death. These infections disproportionately impact communities already facing barriers to care, including immigrants, people with low incomes, people who use drugs, men who have sex with men, and those with histories of homelessness or involvement with the criminal justice system. Every day this initiative reaches people who are often left out of traditional health care systems. Through education and community-based support, we help people

understand hepatitis, get treated and stay engaged in care. The latest data shows both progress and urgency. In 2024, 305 people were newly reported with acute hepatitis B, and 8,029 people were newly reported with a chronic hepatitis B in New York City with ongoing disparities impacting Asian and Pacific Islander and Black communities. For hepatitis C, 398 acute cases were reported, and 2,188 people were newly reported with chronic hepatitis C, the lowest level in a decade, showing that our efforts are working, but we cannot stop here. People are still becoming infected, and too many remain undiagnosed or untreated. If we are serious about eliminating hepatitis B and C in New York City, we must continue to invest in the programs that make treatment and cure possible. The viral hepatitis prevention initiative meets people where they are and does not leave them there. We respectfully ask the Council to sustain funding and approve and additional $2.76 million for a total investment of $5 million. This investment will ensure more New Yorkers are tested, treated and cured. Thank you for your continued

commitment to eliminating hepatitis B and C in New York City.
Thank you. Wen?

Yes. Alright. Hello members of City Council. My name is Charles De San Pedro, Jr., and I have been a member of TOP Clubhouse for seven years and three months. Thank you for having myself and one of TOP’s staff members, Hadley, along with our Director Bianca, and Wen here to testify about our need for funding to keep TOP Clubhouse open. Council Member Cabán, congratulations on your appointment as Chair of the Committee on Mental Health and Substance Use. We have a thrilling invitation for you. We would like you to come to our Clubhouse for an excellent lunch and meet some of our members. Please stop by any week day around 12:30. I have prepared a poem for you and hope that it shows you the love that I have for TOP Clubhouse and proves that I am here for the right reasons. I love TOP. It means so much. And the funding from City Council adds an amazing touch. It allows us to work on the goals we have set and on us, our members have made a safe bet. We’re happy

we’re still open. Us being closed would be sad. When thinking about our members, we know it would make them so mad. Please baseline our funding so we don’t have more stress, and help us make TOP Clubhouse a phenomenal success.
